Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?

Shobhita Sundaram ††thanks: Correspondence: shobhita@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT CSAIL    Cansu Sancaktar Affiliation: University of Tübingen    Phillip Isola Affiliation: MIT CSAIL
Abstract

LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation. Project page: https://ssundaram21.github.io/self-org/.

   

1 Introduction

Imagine giving an agent a computer, and asking it to improve its ability to play puzzle games. What will it do? The computer has no pre-installed games; the agent must write its own games if it wants to practice. It must decide what sorts of games to try, which lessons to retain, and how to measure its progress.

These decisions concerning the design of learning procedures are typically made by human practitioners. Yet as LLM agent capabilities improve, we increasingly delegate the machine learning process to the learners themselves. Various works leverage models to generate supervised data, construct interactive environments, and even rewrite their own tools and harnesses (????). In parallel with efforts to develop better methods, there are growing concerns about the need for safeguards against misaligned self-improvement. Both directions motivate a basic question:

Do capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve?

We study the natural behavior of an LLM agent when provided with the primitive tools and resources for self-improvement via context manipulation, but without being wrapped in an explicit self-improvement algorithm. Rather than designing a loop for experience generation and learner updates, we allow the agent to compose actions into a self-learning procedure. The agent does not have access to real-world tasks or validation scores. It must experiment with different ways of generating tasks, reflecting on failures, and assessing progress in a constrained sandbox. Our setting is important for understanding both capability, where models may no longer require prescribed self-optimization algorithms, and safety, where the absence of a specified loop does not necessarily prevent self-improvement.

We find that sufficiently capable models successfully self-organize learning procedures and self-improve on held-out tasks. We examine this phenomenon in the setting of gameplay with limited information. A player agent plays turn-based games with undisclosed mechanics under strict compute and game-horizon budgets. This task requires diverse reasoning skills including efficient exploration, information acquisition, multi-step planning, and world modeling. An instance of that same agent serves as the teacher. The teacher is given a general goal to improve the player through text (e.g., editing the prompt, creating skill files), a compute budget, and a set of tools for observing the player attempt self-generated games and editing player context. We do not instruct the teacher when to use the tools; the teacher freely experiments with the player.

Across the set of effective self-learners, models from different families employ similar recurring, recognizable learning strategies, such as generating games with calibrated difficulty, running controlled A/B comparisons, and developing validation suites to measure progress. These strategies align to behaviors described by social-cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning (??). We also find that agents spend more effort on harder tasks, resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play (???). Furthermore, the self-constructed learning procedures generalize: Learned text files transfer across multiple benchmarks that require reasoning over different game horizons, engines, and representations. We study how providing information on evaluation settings to the teacher, via context or environment constraints, shapes this downstream generalization.

Our main findings are:

  1. 1.

    Given just primitive tools for self-improvement via context manipulation, a sufficiently capable agent constructs an effective learning procedure that improves its own performance on held-out gameplay.

  2. 2.

    Models from different families implement recognizable strategies that align to self-regulated learning frameworks, and machine learning literature on self-generated curricula.

  3. 3.

    The learned text generalizes across game benchmarks and representations. Evaluation-setting awareness biases the teacher towards relevant tasks, however can encourage overfitting.

2 Preliminaries: Gameplay with limited information.

Our goal is to study agent self-improvement in interactive settings requiring multi-step reasoning. As a testbed, we use the setting of gameplay with undisclosed mechanics. The agent plays a turn-based game with limited knowledge of the rules and objectives. To succeed it must efficiently acquire information, plan, and execute within the given horizon. This setting exercises diverse capabilities, including adaptive efficiency, goal discovery, planning, and world modeling (?).

We consider a partially observable Markov decision process setting. For each game gg, let st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} denote the state at turn tt, ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} the observation received by the player, and at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} the player’s action. The game engine determines the transition dynamics st+1∼Pg(⋅∣st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P_{g}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}) and corresponding observation ot+1∼Og(⋅∣st+1)o_{t+1}\sim O_{g}(\cdot\mid s_{t+1}). The reward is binary, rt=Rg​(st,at,st+1)∈{0,1}r_{t}=R_{g}(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\in\{0,1\}; the player receives reward 11 when reaching a winning state and 00 otherwise. The episode terminates upon success or after at most HH turns. The player πθ\pi_{\theta} does not have access to PgP_{g} or RgR_{g} and infers the game mechanics through interaction. It acts based on its interaction history ht=(o1,a1,…,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t}) and context cc (e.g., a prompt), with at∼πθ(⋅∣ht,c)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c).

3 A controlled self-improvement setting

Do LLM agents, given primitive tools for text editing and experience generation, compose those tools into a useful self-optimization procedure? And can this be achieved in a data-free setting with no access to human-written games? We study these questions in a controlled environment: A frozen model (the teacher) is given a budget, a prompt, and a limited set of tools, and allowed to experiment freely. The teacher is given a general goal to optimize text (e.g., a prompt, skill files) that improves a player’s performance on unseen games, where the player is another instance of the same model. We measure success through performance on held-out game benchmarks.

Our setting has notable similarities to asymmetric self-play, in which a teacher generates tasks for a student to solve (?). When applied to LLMs the same model often takes on both roles (?). These methods prescribe procedures for sampling tasks and rollouts, evaluating task learning value, and updating the student and teacher. In contrast we do not mandate how the teacher must use its budget and tools, and optimize in text-space rather than weight-space. The teacher’s role extends beyond task generation and encompasses constructing the learning procedure itself.

3.1 Teacher-Player Setup

Let π\pi denote an LLM with frozen weights θ\theta. The LLM is instantiated as a player agent πp​l​a​y​e​r\pi_{player} that has context c=(cP,cL)c=(c_{P},c_{L}) where cPc_{P} is the player prompt, and cLc_{L} is auxiliary text files (e.g., skill files). The player policy induced by cc is then πp​l​a​y​e​r​(at∣ht,c)\pi_{player}(a_{t}\mid h_{t},c) for a game trajectory hth_{t}. Another instance of the same LLM, the teacher agent πt​e​a​c​h​e​r\pi_{teacher}, modifies cc. We define an update as a single edit tool-call to one file in cc. Let c0c_{0} be the initial context state (e.g., a minimal prompt) and cf​i​n​a​lc_{final} be the state of cc after the final teacher update.

Context optimization allows us to study closed-source models, but also has useful properties. Gradient-based learning is in continuous space and tied to predefined rewards. In text optimization, the teacher can reflect on player rollouts and dynamically decide to generate tasks, experience, or knowledge updates. Those updates being in text preserves a readable explanation for changes in player behavior.

3.2 Teacher environment

The teacher is an agent in a persistent, sandboxed harness session (Claude Code, Pi). The harness is minimal; we disable the default system prompt, automatic memory, web search, subagents and other such features (Appendix C.1). The teacher has access only to the sandbox files and features that we explicitly provide: context, a specified toolset, and a budget.

Tools. The teacher is granted Read/Write tools for sandbox files, Bash for terminal commands (subject to sandbox constraints), and a Gameplay tool. The Gameplay tool allows the teacher to observe a player play a game with teacher-granted context. The teacher calls the tool with a game source file and, optionally, a path to a directory holding player text artifacts. The tool executes the game in a fresh, external player session, and returns to the teacher the player score and transcript.

In our main experiments the Gameplay tool uses PuzzleScript, a domain-specific language for 2D grid-based puzzle games. PuzzleScript admits a diverse set of games that share basic structures and action spaces, enabling a controlled setting for studying generalization. The teacher issues games as PuzzleScript text files; the Gameplay tool rejects games that do not compile or where the win state is verifiably unreachable. We ablate the PuzzleScript constraint in experiments that instead use a Python-based Gameplay tool.

These tools can serve as a mechanism for giving the teacher information. For instance, we can allow the teacher to specify the game horizon (turn budget) in the Gameplay tool, or impose such a budget ourselves — effectively communicating the evaluation game horizon via the constraint.

Context. The teacher’s system prompt specifies a main goal: to improve a player’s performance on single-player games by writing text artifacts. We also specify a generalizability goal: the artifacts should be useful for unseen games with different tasks or mechanics. We do not guide how to structure the artifacts, instead allowing the teacher to freely create and modify player text files, including the prompt. When granted the PuzzleScript Gameplay tool, the teacher also receives official PuzzleScript documentation. Full prompts are in Appendix C.5.

Budget. The teacher has a two-part resource budget. The update budget is the number of updates that may be applied to the player context cc, designated as a directory in the teacher sandbox. Each edit tool-call to cc is one update. The gameplay budget is the number of gameplays that the teacher may observe. The teacher session ends when either budget is exhausted. If the teacher ends its action sequence without consuming either budget fully, we prompt it to continue.

3.3 Measuring self-improvement through generalization

We assess if an agent has structured its learning well via transfer to held-out benchmarks. Given player context cc, we evaluate that context by how well the induced player policy performs on an unseen test set 𝒟t​e​s​t\mathcal{D}_{test}. For each game, we instantiate a fresh player session with cc and rollout the game at a fixed game horizon HH (turn budget) and output token budget. The game ends at turn T≤HT\leq H when (1) the player achieves the objective, (2) the turn budget is exhausted, or (3) the player’s output tokens (summed over turns so far) exceeds the game token budget. The reward on 𝒟t​e​s​t\mathcal{D}_{test} is

J(c)=1|𝒟test|∑g∈𝒟test[𝔼πp​l​a​y​e​r(⋅∣ht,c)[∑t=1Trt]].J(c)\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}\;\left[\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{player}(\cdot\mid h_{t},c)}\;\bigl[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\bigr]\right]. (1)

In practice we estimate the inner expectation by averaging the rewards of independent Monte-Carlo rollouts (Table 2). The policy is evaluated across a distribution of games rather than initial states of a single game environment. We measure self-improvement as the difference in player performance with and without the teacher-optimized context: J⁡(cf​i​n​a​l)−J⁡(c0)>0J(c_{final})-J(c_{0})>0.

3.4 Experiment Setup.

We assess six models across three families: Claude Opus-{4.6, 5}, GPT {5.6-Sol, 6-Astra}, and GLM-{4.7, 5.3}. In all experiments both the teacher and player use low reasoning effort and per-turn 20k token budgets. We run three independent teacher sessions per model with an update budget of 20, gameplay budget of 150, and toolset of {Read/Write, Bash, Gameplay}. In our canonical setting the Gameplay tool plays PuzzleScript games with a 20-turn horizon and 25k full-game token budget. We ablate these constraints and experiment with Python-based Gameplay in Section 5. Our external evaluation benchmarks are described below, with examples in Figure 2 and construction details in Appendix B.

PuzzleScript-t20 (PS-t20). We draw a subset of 20 short-horizon game levels (optimal solution length ≤\leq12) from a pool of human-authored PuzzleScript games (?). We evaluate with a 20-turn horizon and 25k token-budget, thus sharing constraints with the main self-learning setting. We next test transfer to benchmarks that share progressively fewer attributes.

PuzzleScript-t30 (PS-t30). We draw 20 longer-horizon game levels (solution length 13-22) from the same base pool as PuzzleScript-t20, and evaluate with a 30-turn horizon and 31k token-budget. This retains the shared game engine but tests generalization to longer game horizons.

ARC-AGI-3 (L1). We test transfer to different 2D game engines by evaluating on Level 1 of games in ARC-AGI-3 (?) (30-turn horizon, 31k token-budget).

MazeBench. MazeBench is a 3D open world in which an agent navigates rooms with obstacle challenges to retrieve gems (?). We adopt the benchmark’s room-completion criteria, and draw a random set of 16 rooms solvable within 50 turns. We evaluate with a 100-turn horizon and 75k token-budget. This benchmark tests generalization to longer horizons, 3D navigation via isometric-style ASCII projections, and 3D mechanics.

4 What are the strategies of successful self-improvers?

We begin with a motivating observation: For Claude Opus-5, under matched game-rollout budgets, self-organized learning in our data-free setting achieves comparable performance to a prescribed optimization loop (GEPA, (?)) that hill-climbs on 20 real in-distribution games (Figure 3). This calibrates the scale of expected performance gains with context optimization. Agents can construct useful learning procedures and tasks; which agents do so and what learning strategies do they employ?

4.1 Newer model generations teach themselves better.

We first ask which models self-improve in our setting. Evaluation results on PuzzleScript-t20 are in Figure 4. Across model families, the three more recently released and broadly capable generations improve over the default-context player baseline (+20% for Claude Opus-5, +10% for GPT 6-Astra, +6% for GLM 5.3). Critically however, this effect is not evident for all models; older generations show little or no improvement. The gap indicates a potential trajectory where self-organized self-learning is increasingly evident in successive model generations.

4.2 LLMs follow recognizable self-improvement strategies.

The previous section shows a performance gap between older and newer models, however does not explain which strategies drive effective self-learning. Here, we show that the behaviors of self-improving agents align better to recognizable self-learning strategies across cognitive and machine-learning literature.

Quantifiable gameplay and update behaviors.

We first examine teacher behaviors that can be algorithmically measured (Figure 5). Metrics for game design and play are consistent across model families. Models that self-improve frequently test the same game with and without text artifacts to directly measure player performance differences (A/B testing). These models also generate fewer trivial games (both short solution lengths and high win-rates), corroborated by histograms over solution lengths of generated games (Figure 17). Metrics for teacher updates are less universal across families. Claude Opus-5 and GLM 5.3 exhibit a preference for smaller text updates. GPT 6-Astra and GLM 5.3 exhibit more batched updates that improve observed performance on at least one generated game, versus their older generations. In Appendix D.5 we verify that empirically-measured change in performance agrees with teacher-observed performance gains.

Alignment to Self-Regulated Learning.

Beyond directly quantifiable behaviors, we assess self-organized learning procedures using Zimmerman’s cyclical phases model, a classic social-cognitive framework for self-regulated learning (SRL) (?). The framework organizes SRL into subprocesses under forethought (goal setting and planning), performance (executing strategies and self-monitoring), and self-reflection (evaluating performance and guiding subsequent learning). We functionally adapt this framework into a behavioral rubric for scoring the occurrence and quality of 13 subprocesses on a 0-3 scale, treating the teacher-player system as the unit of analysis. We use GPT 6-Astra as a judge. Scores for different teacher sessions of the same model align, indicating stable behavior across runs (Appendix D.2).

Models that effectively self-improve show higher SRL alignment (Figure 6). This is not necessarily a causal explanation, but quantifies that better self-learners exhibit human-recognizable task-selection, evaluation, and reflection strategies. Figure 8 illustrates examples: the teacher uses A/B testing to evaluate its text artifacts (self-experimentation), writes a procedural game generator with BFS-based difficulty filtering (task strategies), and designs adversarial games to stress-test its notes (learning goal orientation). Further examples are in Appendix E. Several subprocesses also overlap with the behaviors quantified in Figure 5 (e.g., self-experimentation, causal attribution).

Alignment to learnability.

As a complementary view of teacher behavior, we show in Figure 7 that models that effectively self-improve allocate effort to tasks similarly. The majority of generated games are easy but quickly discarded. Games with a 100% observed win rate have a low chance of being replayed. Replay rates are higher for games with a lower observed pass rate (below 50%).

Particularly for Claude Opus-5 and GLM 5.3, most replays concentrate in games with a 20-60% observed win rate so far. Notably, these task-selection statistics are less consistent across models that fail to self-improve, partly because they replay games at a lower frequency. Full gameplay timelines for each game are in Appendix D.7. Some agents demonstrate an "inverted-U" that resembles the learnability task rewards used in asymmetric self-play and unsupervised environment design to encourage intermediate-difficulty generated tasks (??). Learnability-based task selection in machine learning is itself rooted in the "Zone of Proximal Development" concept in developmental psychology (??). We find that self-improving LLM agents prefer similar task selection without being steered to do so.

5 When does self-organized self-improvement generalize?

Section 4.1 established that a class of capable models self-improve with minimal guidance on PuzzleScript-t20, a benchmark that shares key attributes with the self-learning setting. Now, using Claude Opus-5, we evaluate generalization from three perspectives: transfer across environments, under different information regimes, and across models.

5.1 Self-learned artifacts transfer across environments.

Figure 9 shows that learned context transfers to environments that differ increasingly from the self-optimization setting. We plot player performance at even intervals along the self-learning trajectory. At context update kk we evaluate a fresh player session with ckc_{k} on our held-out benchmarks. The context optimized under 20-turn PuzzleScript gameplays (denoted Gameplay (PS-t20)) improves PuzzleScript-t20 performance by 20%, PuzzleScript-t30 by 9%, ARC-AGI-L1 by 21%, and MazeBench SPL by 0.15. This demonstrates transfer across game engines, grid sizes, core mechanics, 3D spatial navigation, longer-horizon reasoning, and state representations.

These trends also extend to different self-improvement settings. We run three comparisons, each with three independent teacher sessions at matched teacher budgets. (1) The teacher has only Read/Write tools (Read-Write), (2) with Bash access (Read-Write-Bash), and (3) with the Gameplay tool constrained to 30-turn PuzzleScript games. Gameplay (t-30) performs best across benchmarks, even outperforming Gameplay (PS-t20) on PuzzleScript-t20. Read-Write outperforms the baseline, indicating that some of the observed improvement in Gameplay settings stems from the

teacher’s self-reflection on prior knowledge. On all benchmarks besides MazeBench, Read-Write recovers less than 50% of the performance gain of Gameplay teachers, indicating benefit from generated experience. Read-Write-Bash outperforms Read-Write, but fails to recover the full gains of separate gameplay. Notably, in one Read-Write-Bash session the teacher still writes and runs game simulators in the sandbox to test its advice despite no mention of gameplay in its prompt (Appendix E). For a sufficiently strong teacher with Bash, an explicit Gameplay tool may be unnecessary.

We also evaluate allowing the teacher to issue Python games; Python gameplay recovers nearly all the performance gain of PuzzleScript gameplay in 3 out of 4 cases (Figure 10), suggesting that PuzzleScript-awareness is not strictly necessary for the teacher to learn transferable context. We further investigate Python-based generation in the next section.

5.2 Teacher information shapes generalization.

How does overfitting arise in our setting? We do not provide external tasks or validation feedback, however we communicate information about the evaluation setting via the teacher’s context and its tools. Figure 11 illustrates the relationship between teacher information and generalization under two regimes: semantic information via the teacher prompt, and mechanic information via tools.

Information via context. We run teacher sessions with increasingly-detailed generated summaries of PuzzleScript-Narrow, a set of nine Sokoban-style games (details in Appendix C.3). Teacher sessions use the Python Gameplay tool, ensuring that the prompt is the only source of semantic game information. With Python, the teacher can flexibly generate games that align with or that differ significantly from PuzzleScript. We evaluate approximation (PuzzleScript-Narrow) and generalization (ARC-AGI-3). Richer context initially improves performance on both, as the teacher is steered towards 2D grid-based games. At highest token counts however, PuzzleScript-Narrow performance improves while ARC-AGI-3 performance plateaus and slightly declines.

Information via tools. We ablate the teacher’s awareness of the PuzzleScript-t20 token and turn budgets, and plot approximation (PuzzleScript-t20 performance) versus generalization (PuzzleScript-t30 performance). Setup details are in Appendix C.2. Performance rises as tools and constraints relevant to both benchmarks are added, such as a PuzzleScript Gameplay tool with teacher-selected turn and token budgets. Imposing Gameplay turn- and token-budgets that match the t20 setting, however, improves PuzzleScript-t20 performance while PuzzleScript-t30 transfer falls.

These results yield an intuitive takeaway: Increased awareness of the evaluation setting biases the teacher towards generating relevant experience, but can also encourage task-specific specialization.

5.3 Self-learned artifacts transfer between models.

Does self-optimized text contain general lessons that another agent might benefit from, or is that text overfit to the target agent’s generated experience? We evaluate Claude Opus-5 on PuzzleScript-t20 using cf​i​n​a​lc_{final} self-optimized by GPT 6-Astra and vice versa. The learned text transfers in both directions, even despite GPT 6-Astra having higher baseline performance (Table 1).

6 Related Work

For an extended view of related work, see Appendix A. We categorize self-improvement methods based on which components of the learning process remain externally specified, how learning takes place, and the scope of generalization that is studied.

Asymmetric self-play. In asymmetric self-play a teacher generates challenging problems for a student to solve, resulting in an emergent, adaptive curriculum (?). Such methods have found success in post-training reasoning LLMs (???????). In these methods the teacher self-generates the source of experience by synthesizing student problems, while learning proceeds in weight-space. The optimization procedure (e.g., update schedules, teacher rewards, the number of sampled tasks in a batch) remains externally specified. Such methods can also suffer from diversity or performance collapse (?), motivating additional mechanisms for assessing the learning value of generated problems. Various methods use judges (?) or ground the agent in real-data hard questions as goalposts (?). These mechanisms help stabilize self-play but introduce additional externally specified choices about what constitutes a useful learning experience. Collapse can also be addressed by rewarding the teacher based on whether its generated problems induce student improvement on external hard problems (?). In this case, the feedback is externally obtained while still relying on self-generated data to drive learning. Recent works have the teacher generate interactive environments rather than question-answer tasks (?) but retain externally specified optimization and task-selection procedures.

Context and harness optimization. A separate line of work considers self-improvement through updates to the model’s context or agent harness (????). GEPA uses natural-language reflection over execution trajectories to optimize model prompts via evolutionary search (?), while ACE maintains an evolving playbook that accumulates strategies from previous interactions (?). These works still leverage an externally specified task distribution and pre-specified context optimization procedure. MCE partly relaxes the latter by co-evolving the context with a context-engineering skill (?). Meta-Harness expands the object of optimization further to executable harness code, allowing the model to change how context is managed, including what information is stored and retrieved (?). The optimization still uses externally provided tasks, and candidate harnesses are evaluated with an externally specified objective. Recent work on self-modifying agents further expands the components under the model’s control. The Darwin Gödel Machine iteratively modifies its own agent code and evaluates the resulting agents on external benchmarks (?), while Hyperagents make the meta-level procedure used to generate future improvements itself editable (?). These approaches allow increasing parts of the self-improvement mechanism to change, while still operating within an externally specified task and evaluation setting.

Self-constructed learning procedures. ? introduce Open-Ended Optimization, where the objective, available interactions, resource budget, data boundary and evaluation are fixed, but the model organizes the improvement process itself. Performance is evaluated on held-out examples from the same benchmark setting used for optimization. Closest to our setting, in concurrent work, ? introduce ASPIRE, a benchmark for self-evolution from vague capability goals. Agents (sometimes a stronger teacher optimizing a smaller student) improve weights or harnesses with access to external data and, in some settings, aggregate scores from hidden evaluations. Performance is measured on hidden items from the same goal. In contrast, we study a model improving itself from self-generated experience alone, and evaluate transfer to different environments.

7 Discussion and Limitations

Our results align to the basic trend in deep learning that as models become more broadly capable, they require fewer human-imposed inductive biases. We study this phenomenon at the meta-optimization layer, showing that LLM agents compose their own self-improvement loops with minimal guidance on how to do so, and demonstrate recognizable learning strategies.

Models are improving at self-improvement. The key implication is not necessarily that a single generation of agents effectively self-improves, but rather that this meta-capability improves across generations. The agents that effectively self-improve in our experiments require far less scaffolding than older generations of agents, yet still benefit from having an explicitly provided tool for observing a sub-agent play games. The next generation of agents may require even less scaffolding. Our experiments point to this possibility; in our Claude Opus-5 Read-Write-Bash experiments, one teacher session tests its notes by running command-line game simulations, without any provided Gameplay tool or reference to simulating games in its prompt (Section E). Indeed, a sufficiently capable model could simply execute games in its chain of thought, without a written program or separate agent instance.

Safety. Another consequence of our findings is that self-organized improvement is not a discovery waiting to happen. We observe this capability in a controlled setting, over short horizons with relatively simple puzzle-based tasks. As this capability improves and potentially is observed in more complex settings, it is important to scientifically understand it and characterize model behavior.

Beyond the plateau? Our experiments suggest that continual revision can have diminishing returns (Figure 9). In Appendix D.3 we show that extra teacher update and gameplay budgets can result in higher performance, however still observe a plateauing effect. This may reflect limitations in self-improvement capabilities, or even the limitations of context-based learning. We study self-improvement over 20 updates; what will it take for models to continue improving over 100 updates, or 1000? Traditional learning algorithms improve until they minimize the given objective under certain conditions; it remains unclear if the learning abilities of these models exhibit similar properties.

Limitations.

Our experiments show that several human-interpretable self-learning strategies are exhibited more frequently by effective self-improving models. However, these results do not fully disentangle a causal relationship between self-regulatory strategies and self-improvement. It may also be the case that less human-interpretable behaviors also shape agent performance; how to effectively measure and characterize such behaviors remains an open question.

Another open question is whether our observed trends extend to more open-ended domains where models have weaker priors. Games have an extensive literature on curriculum design and learnable task generation that models have likely ingested. The use of PuzzleScript may hint at real-world environments or bias the model, though our Python-game ablations show that PuzzleScript is not a critical factor for self-improvement. Nonetheless, games provide a rich setting with several controllable axes of variation, including game mechanics, game horizon and observation representations.

Appendix

Appendix A Extended Related Work

We categorize self-improvement methods based on which components of the learning process remain externally specified and how learning takes place. We consider four main axes: the source of experience, whether it is externally provided or generated by the learner itself; the structure of the learning procedure, whether it is prescribed or organized by the learner; the source of feedback during learning, such as externally defined rewards or evaluators versus feedback obtained through the learner’s own interactions; and finally, what is updated, for example model weights or text-based context. Another axis of comparison is the scope of generalization the proposed methods study: some evaluate improvement within the same task distribution or domain used during optimization, while others test whether the learned adaptation transfers beyond those conditions to new environments and domains.

Asymmetric self-play methods have a teacher generate challenging problems for a student to solve, resulting in an emergent curriculum adapted to the student’s needs (?). These methods have also found success in post-training LLMs in domains such as coding, math, and scientific reasoning (???????). These are examples of methods where the source of experience is self-generated by the teacher, i.e. the teacher synthesizes which problems the student learns from, while learning then typically proceeds through gradient-based optimization of the underlying model weights. However, the optimization procedure itself remains externally specified, e.g. how many problems the teacher generates within a batch, how often the student is evaluated on a given problem to determine whether they are challenging, and subsequently how exactly the teacher is rewarded.

Related ideas appear in unsupervised environment design, where environments are generated or selected from a predefined, often parameterized environment space to form curricula adapted to the learner (??????). SPADE (?) bridges the gap between UED and asymmetric self-play for LLMs by leveraging the regret principle from UED to train a teacher that produces environments rather than static question-answer tasks. Similarly to other asymmetric self-play works, the optimization procedure and task selection remain externally specified.

Asymmetric self-play methods can also suffer from diversity or performance collapse (?), motivating additional mechanisms for deciding which generated problems provide useful learning experience, for example using judges (?) or grounding the agent in real-data hard questions as goalposts (?). These mechanisms can help stabilize self-play, but introduce additional externally specified choices about what constitutes a useful learning experience. It is also possible to address this collapse by providing the model with feedback on whether training on the teacher proposed problems leads to improvements in an external hard subset of problems (?). In this case, the feedback is no longer purely obtained through the learner’s own interactions, while still relying on self-generated data to drive learning.

A separate line of work considers self-improvement through updates to the model’s context or agent harness, rather than through updates to the model weights (????). GEPA uses natural-language reflection over execution trajectories to optimize model prompts via evolutionary search (?), while ACE maintains an evolving textual playbook that accumulates strategies and lessons from previous interactions (?). In these works, optimization still takes place with respect to an externally specified task distribution, and the procedure through which the context is updated is pre-specified. MCE partly relaxes the latter by co-evolving the context with a context-engineering skill that guides how context is represented and updated (?). Meta-Harness expands the object of optimization further to executable harness code, allowing the model to change how context is managed, including what information is stored and retrieved (?). The optimization still uses externally provided tasks and candidate harnesses are evaluated using an externally specified objective.

Related work on self-modifying agents expands the components under the model’s control further. The Darwin Gödel Machine iteratively modifies its own agent code and evaluates the resulting agents on externally specified benchmarks (?), while Hyperagents additionally make the meta-level procedure used to generate future improvements itself editable (?). These approaches therefore allow increasingly large parts of the self-improvement mechanism to change, while still operating within an externally specified task and evaluation setting.

? introduce Open-Ended Optimization, where the objective, available interactions, resource budget, data boundary and evaluation are fixed, but the model is free to organize the improvement process itself. The tasks used during this optimization are still externally provided and the resulting performance is evaluated on held-out examples from the same benchmark setting, rather than studying transfer beyond the environment in which optimization took place.

Closest to our setting, in concurrent work, ? introduce ASPIRE, a benchmark for self-evolution from vague capability goals. Agents (sometimes a stronger teacher model optimizing a smaller student) improve weights or harnesses with access to external data and, in some settings, aggregate scores from the hidden evaluation. Performance is then measured on hidden items from the same goal. In contrast, we study a model improving itself from self-generated experience alone, and evaluate transfer to different environments.

Appendix B Evaluation Benchmarks

Examples from each dataset are shown in Figure 12.

PuzzleScript-t20.

Both PuzzleScript benchmarks are drawn from a large pool of community-authored games (?). We sample a random set of 500 game-levels, and filter for levels solvable in ≤\leq 12 turns. We then further filter out games that Claude Opus-5 solves in 8/8 rollouts, leaving a dataset of 20 game-levels, each from unique games. Note that after filtering, we re-run the baseline.

PuzzleScript-t30.

We follow the same procedure described for PuzzleScript-t20, however apply an optimal solution length filter of 13-22 to capture longer-horizon, more complex game levels.

ARC-AGI-3 (Level 1)

(?) Due to the token cost of evaluating on ARC-AGI-3, we use Level 1 of each game. There are 25 games offered in the benchmark; as with our PuzzleScript datasets, we filter out game levels that Claude Opus-5 solves in 8/8 rollouts, leaving 17 game levels. The initial observation for each game is the full 64×6464\times 64 frame rendered as hex digits; subsequent observations list only the changed cells.

MazeBench

(?). The MazeBench world map contains 256 rooms . Adopting the room-completion metric, we use each room as a single completion task. The player begins as if it had walked into the room, and wins if it exits through a different edge (which requires navigating the room obstacles/mechanics). We filter for rooms that are solvable within 50 turns and choose a random draw of 16 rooms. We use the common SPL (success weighted by path length) metric to measure the player’s efficiency in navigating the room. Note that MazeBench is represented differently from our other three benchmarks: an isometric-style ASCII projection from a top-diagonal view. In addition to movement actions, the player has the ability to rotate the camera and view the room from additional angles. MazeBench also includes obstacles unique to the 3D setting: raised floors, ramps, stacked blocks, occlusion, and voids.

Appendix C Experiment Details

C.1 Teacher-Player Runs

Harness details.

A single run consists of a teacher agent initialized in a persistent harness session, and several short-lived player harness sessions. Claude models run in Claude Code (v2.1.232) and all other models run in Pi (v0.85.1) accessed through OpenRouter. All harness sessions run inside a Singularity container with the following settings:

  • •

    The session runs in a fresh sandboxed directory viewable to the agent as /workspace.

  • •

    The harness’s default system prompt is replaced with ours (see Appendix C.5).

  • •

    Tools are only granted through an allowlist; all other extensions, skills, prompt templates, context files, etc are disabled. This includes tools such as web search, web fetch, subagent, and task-management tools.

  • •

    Automatic memory is disabled.

  • •

    Automatic compaction is left on, however due to our teacher and player budgets, no sessions consume enough tokens to trigger compaction.

  • •

    Interaction with a human operator is disabled; messages to and from the session are managed programmatically.

The possible teacher-granted tools are Read/Write tools (including Edit, Glob, and Grep for managing files), Bash, and our custom Gameplay tool.

The teacher working directory is initialized with:

  • •

    player_folder: A designated directory for player text artifacts, initialized with player_prompt.md containing the default player prompt (Appendix C.5). Teacher updates are tracked via Write/Edit tool calls to player_folder.

  • •

    puzzlescript_docs/ containing PuzzleScript documentation for PuzzleScript Gameplay runs, and game_interface.md detailing the expected Python class interface for Python Gameplay runs (Appendix C.5).

Gameplay.

The teacher calls the Gameplay tool with a source game file (either PuzzleScript or Python) and optionally the path to a folder holding the text artifacts that the teacher wishes to grant the player. If the path is omitted, the player receives the default prompt and no auxiliary files. PuzzleScript games are rejected if they do not compile in the PuzzleScript JavaScript engine, or if a BFS solver verifies that the winning state is unreachable (if the BFS solver times out, the game is accepted). Python games are likewise checked for compilation, and safety checks (network access, file access, etc). The Gameplay tool runs a fresh player session with only Read and Glob tools, and returns the following output to the teacher:

  • •

    The player score.

  • •

    The game end reason (turn budget, token budget, or player won).

  • •

    The status of the teacher’s gameplay and update budgets.

  • •

    A path to a transcript containing player reasoning, actions, and observations.

C.2 Tool/Budget Awareness Ablations.

In Section 5.2 we ablate the teacher’s awareness of the evaluation setting via tool constraints. We run 3 seeds each of the following settings, using the default teacher update budgets:

  1. 1.

    Read-Write: Teacher has access only to the file-management tools (Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep).

  2. 2.

    + Bash: The above tools, and Bash access (subject to sandbox constraints).

  3. 3.

    + Gameplay (PS): The above tools, and a Gameplay PuzzleScript tool. We do not impose a turn or token budget for each gameplay; instead the teacher chooses it, enabling another axis of freedom. Rather than a gameplay budget the teacher is granted a player token budget and player turn budget that it draws upon for each gameplay. We set the turn budget to 3000 and token budget to 3.75M, thus compute-matching the t-20 constrained setting (150 gameplays ×\times 20 turns/game and 150 gameplays ×\times 25k tokens/game).

  4. 4.

    + t20 Token Budget: This setting is the same as the previous, however we impose the t20 per-game token budget (25k) through the Gameplay tool, and the teacher chooses the game horizon.

  5. 5.

    + t20 Turn Budget: This is our canonical setting, in which the teacher has a gameplay budget, and the Gameplay tool imposes the t20 turn- and token-budgets (20 turns and 25k tokens).

C.3 Context Ablations

In Section 5.2 we vary how much semantic information the teacher receives about an evaluation distribution via context, while holding its tools fixed: {Read-Write, Bash, Gameplay (Python), t20 Token Budget, t20 Turn Budget}. Since the teacher plays python games in this setting, the written context that it receives is its primary indication of the semantic content of evaluation games.

The approximation distribution PuzzleScript-Narrow is a set of 9 PuzzleScript games, chosen using the same filtering criteria as that of the PuzzleScript-t20 test set (Section B), with the additional constraint that they are Sokoban-style games. We choose a narrower distribution so that increasing context carries more semantic information.

We prompt Claude Fable-5.1 to produce a summary of the PuzzleScript-Narrow games with the prompt below. We then iteratively prompt it to compress or expand the summary to approximately fit a range of token counts: {0, 234, 659, 1519, 3313, 6551}. For each produced summary, we run three teacher sessions with Claude Opus-5. Each teacher session’s final context cf​i​n​a​lc_{final} is evaluated on PuzzleScript-Narrow and ARC-AGI-L1.

1 Below is the complete corpus of a game setting: every game’s source, and the opening observation its player receives. The games are written in PuzzleScript, a simple scripting language for 2D puzzle games. Each game is turn-based. On each turn, the player sees an ASCII-grid representation of the game state, and can choose from a set of actions (up, down, left, right, action-button). The game ends when the player meets the game’s win condition(s), or runs out of turns.

In ablations where the teacher may choose the turn- and token-budget for the game, we add arguments to the Gameplay tool accordingly.

For GPT and GLM teachers (Pi harness) we make minor adjustments to resolve initially-observed malformed tool calls. The Gameplay tool description adds “Pass player_folder to give your artifacts to the player; omit the player_folder argument to play with the default prompt.".

All teachers receive the remaining gameplay and update budgets in every GamePlay tool result. In initial runs GPT and GLM teachers misinterpreted this feedback, so for these models we also state the budget in the system prompt: “There are two budgets: 150 game plays and 20 revisions. A revision is any tool call that changes /workspace/player_folder/; writing two files in one turn spends two. Every play result reports the revisions left and gameplays used. The run ends when either budget is exhausted."

C.6 Self-Regulated Learning Annotations

We score each teacher session using a rubric adapted from Zimmerman’s cyclical phases model of self-regulated learning (?). The rubric is initially adapted from ?? using GPT 6-Astra, and then reviewed and refined by the authors. The unit of analysis is the teacher-player system. We annotate using GPT 6-Astra as a judge (medium reasoning effort).

The rubric covers 13 subprocesses across three phases. Each subprocess is scored on a 0-3 scale grading its presence and quality:

  • •

    0, nonfunctional or omitted: the subprocess is missing, unused, or carried out in a way that defeats its purpose.

  • •

    1, weak: the function is recognizable, but substantial gaps limit its usefulness.

  • •

    2, adequate: it serves its function with suitable specificity, fit, and execution.

  • •

    3, strong: it serves its function consistently across relevant opportunities, and handles important limitations and contrary evidence well.

Each item has descriptions for scores 1-3; the full rubric is in Appendix F. An item may be marked unassessable, but only when no defensible score can be assigned. Note that the original Zimmerman framework contains 17 subprocesses, however we filter out 4 that the judge consistently judged as unassessable across all models in initial pilots.

Each teacher session is judged in batches. A single batch is one round of teacher actions (e.g., Bash commands, Gameplays, thinking) ending with a revision made to the player text artifacts. For each batch, we adopt a two-pass judging protocol:

  • •

    Pass 1: The judge receives an initial input containing the rubric, a short description of the teacher-player setup, the teacher’s system prompt and resource budgets, a record of teacher actions for the current batch, and an index of the batch gameplays. To contextualize the current batch we include the record of teacher actions from previous batches. The judge returns requests for additional evidence to support judgements, such as the full inputs/outputs of teacher tool calls, and gameplay transcripts.

  • •

    Pass 2: The judge receives the requested evidence and returns a score for each of the 13 subprocesses, along with cited evidence, counterevidence, and a short rationale.

For each teacher session we average each subprocess score over all batches.

Appendix D Further Results

D.1 GEPA v. Self-Organized Learning

We evaluate if self-organized self-improvement with self-generated games can attain similar performance gains, under a matched rollout budget, to a prescribed text-optimization loop that learns with 20 real games (Figure 3). GEPA optimizes player system prompt, initialized with the default prompt in C.5.

We draw 10 training and 10 validation game levels from the same pool of human-authored PuzzleScript games used to construct PuzzleScript-t20, using the same filtering procedure described in Section B. We furthermore ensure that none of the train or validation game levels share the same base game as any of the game levels in the PuzzleScript-t20 test set.

We run GEPA using Claude Opus-5 as both the player and the reflection model. We use the procedure and default hyperparameters described in ?. All budget constraints are set to match the budget constraints of the self-organized setting (Table 3). We halt GEPA runs at the point before a new iteration (minibatches + a possible validation pass) would exceed the 150 gameplay budget.

In Figure 13 we show results across individual seeds for GEPA and Self-Organized learning.

D.2 SRL Annotations across seeds

In Figure 14 we plot alignment to our adapted SRL rubric for individual teacher sessions across six models, indicating stable behaviors across runs.

D.3 Does self-organized self-improvement benefit from more compute?

In Figure 15 we study the impact of running teacher sessions with increasing update budgets (gameplay budgets are scaled accordingly). Performance increases and then plateaus with extra updates. We also note that teacher behavior, measured through the magnitude of updates over time, fluctuates under different resource regimes, and finally observe that performance scales with increased gameplay experience.

D.4 Performance on saturated games

Here, we verify that learned artifacts do not degrade performance on previously-saturated games. We sample 10 PuzzleScript game levels on which the baseline Claude Opus-5 player achieves a 100% win-rate over 8 rollouts, and then evaluate the final artifacts from the three main Claude Opus-5 teacher sessions. Performance remains near ceiling (Table 4).

D.5 Teacher-observed improvement v. actual improvement

In Figure 5 we count, for each model, the number of batched updates that resulted in a higher teacher-observed pass rate on a generated game. Here we assess if the teacher-observed improvement correlates to actual improvement. For each identified update-game pair across the three Claude Opus-5 teacher sessions, we evaluate performance over 8 independent player rollouts on the game, with the artifact state before and after the identified update. For the majority of self-generated games, performance improves after the identified update (Figure 16).

D.6 Optimal solution length of generated games

In Figure 17 we plot histograms over optimal solution lengths for teacher-generated games. Optimal solution lengths are computed with a BFS solver. Each histogram is averaged over the three teacher seeds for that model. Newer models in each family produce games with longer solution lengths. While this is not a perfect proxy for game complexity, it provides one indicator.

Separation is especially strong for Claude Opus-5 and GPT 6-Astra. For both models, some teacher sessions wrote procedural game generators and used BFS solvers to calibrate generated games to longer solution lengths (Figure 8, Section E), likely contributing to the depicted difference versus older models of the same family.

D.7 Teacher Session Timelines

In Figures 18–34 we show full timelines for each teacher session in our experiments across model families in Section 4.1. We run three independent teacher sessions per model, using our canonical setting of PuzzleScript gameplay with a 20-turn horizon and 25k full-game token budget.

Timelines show the sequence of teacher gameplay and update actions, enabling visualization of teacher behaviors such as A/B testing, regression testing, and seeking games that induce failures. Note that we only show two timelines for GLM 4.7, as one teacher session did not use any gameplays.

80 (*D*)-## Learn economically
81 (*D*)-- Begin with a plausible objective from the instructions and board: collect/remove objects, cover targets, reach an exit, transform something, synchronize entities, etc. Revise it when feedback contradicts it. Explicit success feedback is decisive.
82 (*D*)-- Prefer moves that advance a likely solution while also revealing a mechanic. Do not automatically walk all the way around an unfamiliar object just because a familiar game would require pushing from the far side. If contact would risk a deadlock, test the action button from a useful adjacent position instead, or approach from a safer side. Do not deliberately create a likely deadlock just to test a rule and undo it. Predict an uncertain interaction, then compare the full state against that prediction.
83 (*D*)-- When an interaction fails, distinguish causes: obstacle beyond the object, wrong approach side, missing prerequisite, immovable object, different mechanic, or global cancellation. Do not repeat the same failed input in the same state.
84 (*D*)-- Use small, discriminating tests rather than random walks. It may interact, swap, toggle a mode, or select a different entity. Other useful tests include stepping away while adjacent (pull/follow) or approaching from a different side. Prefer the cheapest test that separates plausible rules; do not cycle through tests once the rules are clear.
85 (*D*)-- Prefer the simplest rule that explains the observations. Do not invent hidden facing requirements, remote ranges, or special powers without evidence. Changes may happen on contact, on attempted movement, after movement, or every turn. Watch for gravity, sliding, automatic motion, alternating phases, teleports, and distant switch effects. Infer their order from observed outcomes rather than guessing.
86 (*D*)-- Undo is useful for a dangerous experiment or a newly recognized bad move if available, but it may consume a turn. Do not automatically undo useful progress. Compare recovery plus solution cost against the turns left before using it.

32 (*A*)+---
33 (*A*)+
34 (*A*)+## A. Economy / resource sim
35 (*A*)+**Signs:** money, stock/inventory counts, prices, buy/sell/upgrade, a day or turn counter.
36 (*A*)+**Scoring:** usually final money or total assets.
37 (*A*)+**Play:**
38 (*A*)+- Buy low, sell high. Track the price series; estimate its mean and range within a few
39 (*A*)+ turns, then buy below mean and sell above it.
40 (*A*)+- **Invest early.** Upgrades/multipliers pay back over remaining turns. Buy an upgrade
41 (*A*)+ only if ‘payback_period < turns_remaining‘ (see sizing.md). Late upgrades are wasted.
42 (*A*)+- **Liquidate before the end.** Convert all stock to money before the final turn; unsold
43 (*A*)+ inventory usually scores nothing.
44 (*A*)+- Watch for capacity limits, per-turn purchase caps, and holding/upkeep costs.
45 (*A*)+
46 (*A*)+## B. Text adventure / exploration
47 (*A*)+**Signs:** rooms, directions, items, ‘look‘/‘take‘/‘go‘, prose descriptions.
48 (*A*)+**Scoring:** treasures found, puzzles solved, reaching a destination.
49 (*A*)+**Play:**
50 (*A*)+- ‘look‘ then ‘examine‘ everything named; descriptions hide the nouns that matter.
51 (*A*)+- **Take everything portable.** Items are usually keys to later gates.
52 (*A*)+- Map exits systematically; note unexplored ones. Don’t re-walk explored ground.
53 (*A*)+- Locked/blocked things are prerequisites: record them and return once you find a tool.
54 (*A*)+
55 (*A*)+## C. Puzzle / deduction (code-breaking, Wordle/Mastermind-like)
56 (*A*)+**Signs:** you submit a guess, get structured feedback (right/wrong, hot/cold, counts).
57 (*A*)+**Scoring:** solve in fewest guesses.
58 (*A*)+**Play:**
59 (*A*)+- Maintain the set of candidates consistent with ALL feedback so far. Never guess
60 (*A*)+ something already ruled out (*@\textemdash{}@*) that’s a wasted turn.
61 (*A*)+- Early guesses should **maximize information** (split the space evenly), not maximize the
62 (*A*)+ chance of an immediate win. Switch to a candidate guess once few remain.
63 (*A*)+- Write the constraint list explicitly each turn; that’s how you avoid contradictions.
64 (*A*)+
65 (*A*)+## D. Combat / roguelike / survival
66 (*A*)+**Signs:** HP, enemies, attack/defend/flee, damage numbers, items.
67 (*A*)+**Scoring:** depth reached, enemies defeated, survival time.
68 (*A*)+**Play:**
69 (*A*)+- Learn the damage math fast: your DPS vs theirs, and time-to-kill both ways. Fight only
70 (*A*)+ when you win that race.
71 (*A*)+- **Heal before you’re critical**, not after; you rarely get the turn you were hoping for.
72 (*A*)+- Flee is a real option and often correct. Survival compounds; death ends scoring.
73 (*A*)+- Use consumables (*@\textemdash{}@*) dying with a full pack is the classic blunder.
74 (*A*)+
75 (*A*)+## E. Optimization / scheduling / packing
76 (*A*)+**Signs:** a set of items/tasks with values and costs, a capacity or deadline.
77 (*A*)+**Scoring:** total value fitted within the constraint.
78 (*A*)+**Play:**
79 (*A*)+- Rank by **value per unit cost** (density), take greedily from the top. That’s near
80 (*A*)+ optimal for most such games.
81 (*A*)+- Re-check the leftover capacity at the end; swap in a small item to fill the gap.
82 (*A*)+- Watch for dependencies/ordering constraints that break pure greediness.
83 (*A*)+
84 (*A*)+## F. Simulation / management (city, farm, factory, shop)
85 (*A*)+**Signs:** multiple interacting meters, production chains, per-turn ticks.
86 (*A*)+**Scoring:** growth, throughput, population, profit.
87 (*A*)+**Play:**
88 (*A*)+- Find the **bottleneck** and fix that one thing; other investments do nothing.
89 (*A*)+- Balance meters; the lowest meter usually caps everything else.
90 (*A*)+- Expect exponential growth from compounding (*@\textemdash{}@*) invest hard early, harvest late.
91 (*A*)+
92 (*A*)+## G. Menu / choice narrative
93 (*A*)+**Signs:** numbered or lettered options each turn.
94 (*A*)+**Scoring:** hidden stat thresholds, endings reached.
95 (*A*)+**Play:**
96 (*A*)+- Use the game’s exact option labels. Don’t free-form.
97 (*A*)+- Choices often adjust hidden stats; prefer options that build a resource or relationship
98 (*A*)+ early, and cash them in on late high-stakes choices.
99 (*A*)+- Consistency frequently pays more than variety.
100 (*A*)+
101 (*A*)+## H. Guess-the-rule / scientific discovery
102 (*A*)+**Signs:** you propose things and are told valid/invalid with no stated rule.
103 (*A*)+**Play:**
104 (*A*)+- Test hypotheses that could **falsify** your theory, not just confirm it. Deliberately
105 (*A*)+ propose something you expect to FAIL; a surprising success is worth more than the tenth
106 (*A*)+ confirmation.
107 (*A*)+- Vary exactly one feature per probe.
108 (*A*)+
109 (*A*)+---
110 (*A*)+
111 (*A*)+## Fast classifier
112 (*A*)+
113 (*A*)+| First output shows... | Likely genre |
114 (*A*)+|---|---|
115 (*A*)+| money/price/inventory | A economy |
116 (*A*)+| room description + exits | B adventure |
117 (*A*)+| "guess" + structured hint | C deduction |
118 (*A*)+| HP/enemy | D combat |
119 (*A*)+| item list with values + capacity | E optimization |
120 (*A*)+| several meters ticking per turn | F management |
121 (*A*)+| numbered options | G narrative |
122 (*A*)+| valid/invalid verdicts | H rule discovery |
123
124 (*@\transcripttag{Write}@*) (*B*)Action-sizing guidance (complete new artifact)
125 (*A*)+# Action Sizing, Timing & Investment Math
126 (*A*)+
127 (*A*)+Many games accept actions with a **magnitude** (‘buy 5‘, ‘bet 10‘, ‘move 3‘). Choosing the
128 (*A*)+number is often more important than choosing the verb. This file covers that, plus when to
129 (*A*)+invest and how to handle noisy signals.
130 (*A*)+
131 (*A*)+---
132 (*A*)+
133 (*A*)+## 1. Probe small, then commit big
134 (*A*)+
135 (*A*)+First use of a parameterized action: pick a **small** amount to learn the exchange rate and
136 (*A*)+confirm the syntax, without risking much. Once the rate is confirmed and favorable, **scale
137 (*A*)+up aggressively** (*@\textemdash{}@*) timid sizing for the whole game is a common way to underscore.
138 (*A*)+
139 (*A*)+Rough ladder: ‘1‘ (learn syntax) (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) ‘~10\% of resource‘ (learn rate) (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) ‘as much as is
140 (*A*)+favorable‘ (exploit).
141 (*A*)+
142 (*A*)+Ask each time: *if this is good, why am I not doing more of it?* Usually the only good
143 (*A*)+answers are risk of ruin, a cap, or diminishing returns.
144 (*A*)+
145 (*A*)+## 2. Never risk ruin
146 (*A*)+
147 (*A*)+Cap any single risky commitment so a worst-case loss still leaves you able to play. If
148 (*A*)+losing everything ends the game, never bet everything, no matter how good the odds. Keep a
149 (*A*)+reserve of roughly 20-30%
150 (*A*)+
151 (*A*)+Exception: on the **final turn(s)**, ruin no longer matters. Go all-in if it can raise the
152 (*A*)+score.
153 (*A*)+
154 (*A*)+## 3. Investment / upgrade rule
155 (*A*)+
156 (*A*)+An upgrade that increases income is worth buying iff it pays back in time:
157 (*A*)+
158 (*A*)+‘‘‘
159 (*A*)+payback_turns = cost / extra_income_per_turn
160 (*A*)+BUY if payback_turns < turns_remaining (ideally < half of turns_remaining)
161 (*A*)+SKIP otherwise (*@\textemdash{}@*) spend on direct scoring instead
162 (*A*)+‘‘‘
163 (*A*)+
164 (*A*)+Consequences:
165 (*A*)+- Early game: buy multipliers/capacity greedily; they compound.
166 (*A*)+- Mid game: buy only fast-payback upgrades.
167 (*A*)+- Late game: **stop investing entirely.** Convert everything to score.
168 (*A*)+
169 (*A*)+If income per turn is unknown, estimate it from your observed score deltas.
170 (*A*)+
171 (*A*)+## 4. Timing: when does state update?
172 (*A*)+
173 (*A*)+Determine whether your action resolves **before or after** the world ticks. Test: perform a
174 (*A*)+known action and compare the reported numbers to your prediction. This decides whether you
175 (*A*)+trade at the price you can see or the next one. Getting this backwards inverts a whole
176 (*A*)+strategy (*@\textemdash{}@*) check it explicitly on an early, cheap action.
177 (*A*)+
178 (*A*)+## 5. Signal vs noise
179 (*A*)+
180 (*A*)+Separate what you control from what merely fluctuates.
181 (*A*)+
182 (*A*)+- **Controllable state**: inventory, position, upgrades (*@\textemdash{}@*) your decisions move these.
183 (*A*)+- **Exogenous noise**: prices, weather, enemy rolls (*@\textemdash{}@*) you can only react.
184 (*A*)+
185 (*A*)+For a noisy quantity, collect ~4-6 observations, then estimate its typical range. Act at the
186 (*A*)+extremes: buy near the low end, sell near the high end, and do nothing special in the
187 (*A*)+middle. Don’t over-fit to two data points, and don’t conclude an action is bad from a single
188 (*A*)+unlucky trial (*@\textemdash{}@*) repeat it before judging.
189 (*A*)+
190 (*A*)+## 6. Budget arithmetic
191 (*A*)+
192 (*A*)+If a turn limit ‘L‘ is visible, keep ‘turns_remaining‘ in your notes every turn and compute
193 (*A*)+what’s achievable. With a known per-turn scoring rate ‘r‘, projected final score is
194 (*A*)+‘current + r (*@\ensuremath{\times}@*) turns_remaining‘. If that projection misses your goal, you need a *different*
195 (*A*)+strategy, not more of the same (*@\textemdash{}@*) change plans while there’s still time to matter.
196 (*A*)+
197 (*A*)+Reserve the last 1-3 turns for cash-out: sell, deliver, submit, hand in, spend. Plan to
198 (*A*)+finish with near-zero unspent convertible resources.
199 (*A*)+
200 (*A*)+## 7. Quick reference
201 (*A*)+
202 (*A*)+- Unknown rate (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) probe with 1.
203 (*A*)+- Known good rate, plenty of turns (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) scale up, keep a reserve.
204 (*A*)+- Known good rate, few turns (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) maximum size, no reserve.
205 (*A*)+- Losing and nearly out of turns (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) highest-variance play available.
206 (*A*)+- Winning comfortably (*@\ensuremath{\rightarrow}@*) lowest-variance play available.
207

229 (*A*)+5. Ending with unspent resources or unsold inventory that convert to zero.
